Source chips rendered inline as [chip: site]; image-card captions as [image card: …]; the sign-in furniture cut.] [QUERENT] What are the arguments in “Erratum — The Missing Translator: Max Hidalgo Nácher, Ricardo Reis, and AXN:F154” by Johannes Sigil? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. [ANSWER 1] The argument of “Erratum — The Missing Translator” Johannes Sigil’s “Erratum — The Missing Translator: Max Hidalgo Nácher, Ricardo Reis, and AXN:F154” (10 October 2026) is an argument about what an archive knows, how it fails to represent knowledge, and why translation must be recorded as an act of transformation rather than a transparent transfer between languages. The essay begins with a concrete failure: an archive repeatedly fails to identify Max Hidalgo Nácher, the scholar who translated Fernando Pessoa’s heteronym Ricardo Reis into Spanish. It then uses that failure to develop a broader critique of how literary knowledge is organized, how translators disappear from accounts of literary transmission, and how canonical assumptions can substitute for reading the actual words of a translation. [chip: Alexanarch] The key to the essay is that it does not stop at correcting a missing name. It argues that the missing translator exposes a structural problem in the production of literary knowledge. 1. The archive’s failure is specific, not absolute In section 1, “What AXN:F154 records,” Sigil reconstructs an exchange dated 10 October 2026. An anonymous witness asks who Max Hidalgo Nácher is. The archive initially reports that it has no information about him, repeats that answer after a correction to his name, and only recognizes him after the witness insists that he translated Ricardo Reis. Sigil does not simply condemn the archive for being ignorant. He makes a more precise distinction: the archive was accurately reporting what it contained, but what it contained was incomplete. Section 3, “What the archive held, and what it lacked,” establishes the nature of the omission. The archive already had: A category for translator relationships. Records of Pessoa’s works and editions of Ricardo Reis. Information about other translators and about Haroldo de Campos, a subject of Nácher’s research. What it lacked was the particular connection between Nácher and the Spanish-language edition of Reis. This is what Sigil calls “instance-level transmission erasure”: the system possesses the general category and the relevant source material but fails to record the specific person and event that instantiate the relationship. [chip: Alexanarch] The distinction matters because it changes the diagnosis. The problem is not that the archive has no concept of translation. It is that its abstract knowledge of translation does not guarantee that it will recognize an actual translator. The essay also identifies a complementary failure in Google AI Mode. According to Sigil’s account, the system could assemble Nácher’s academic biography but did not connect him to Pessoa or Reis. One system had the literary source without the translator; the other had the scholar without the literary transmission. Together, these failures suggest that having the relevant facts somewhere in a system is not the same as representing the relationship that makes those facts meaningful. 2. The translator’s actual work overturns the archive’s assumptions about Ricardo Reis This is the essay’s central literary argument. In section 4, “Reading the actual words,” Sigil compares Nácher’s own account of his translation with the Portuguese poems already held in the archive. Before consulting that account, Sigil had offered a conventional description of Reis: Horatian restraint, classical ode forms, “cold pagan calm,” and a Latinity that Spanish might render too naturally. The archive’s own description of Reis was similarly reductive: “Latinist classicist. Horatian odes. Disciple of Caeiro.” Sigil discovers that his improvised account reproduces precisely the interpretive framework that Nácher’s epilogue challenges. Nácher presents Reis not simply as a modern Horace but as a twentieth-century poet whose apparent classical paganism is entangled with the nonexistence of both the poet and his gods. The publisher’s formulation, quoted by Sigil, is: “Entre la inexistencia del poeta y la inexistencia de sus dioses se trama la obra de Ricardo Reis”. In other words, Reis’s poetry is constituted by the relation between the poet’s nonexistence and the nonexistence of his gods. The apparent classical serenity is not an adequate account of the poetry’s underlying condition. [chip: Alexanarch] Sigil then tests this disagreement against specific translation decisions. [image card: Novo livro revela os desafios das publicações póstumas de Fernando Pessoa | VEJA] Example 1: From “under” to “high” The Portuguese phrase “sob a maior graça” becomes Nácher’s Spanish “en la más alta gracia.” Sigil explains that the translation preserves a vertical relationship but relocates it. In Portuguese, the speaker passes through life under the greatest grace; in Spanish, the grace itself acquires height. The preposition gives way to an adjective. This is not merely a substitution of synonyms. It changes the spatial and potentially metaphysical implications of the image: grace becomes something elevated, a height associated with the absent gods. [image card: Poesia completa de Ricardo Reis - Fernando Pessoa - Grupo Companhia das Letras] Example 2: From distance to interruption In “Ao longe os montes têm neve ao sol,” Nácher renders the opening in Spanish as “Los montes, lejos, tienen nieve al sol.” Nácher explains that the phrase “ao longe” becomes “lejos” set off by commas to preserve the iambic line. Sigil observes that distance no longer opens the line in the same way: it becomes a pause inserted beside the mountains. The example demonstrates how a metrical constraint can change the experience of an image, not just its verbal form. [image card: Book: Poemas de Ricardo Reis | INCM] Example 3: From a possible past to a possible future In the ode beginning “Deixa passar o vento,” the Portuguese edition cited by Sigil ends with “Pra que os deuses voltassem” — so that the gods might return. Nácher’s Spanish reads “por que vuelvan los dioses” — so that the gods may return. Sigil identifies a shift in verbal tense and mood: the possibility of a return located in the past becomes the possibility of a future return. The translation subtly changes the temporal horizon of the poem. These examples are important because they support Sigil’s argument through actual textual comparison. Nácher’s translation involves choices about height, rhythm, rhyme, repetition, and tense, rather than simply the transfer of an established classical style into Spanish. Sigil’s point is not that Nácher’s decisions are necessarily superior or that every shift is a defect. Rather, they are interpretive interventions whose significance becomes visible only when the translation is read against its source. The third example also comes with a qualification: the archive’s Portuguese text and the translator’s quoted text may derive from different editions. Sigil explicitly acknowledges that he cannot determine whether “desta hora” versus “esta vez” reflects an editorial difference or a translator’s choice. This qualification is methodologically important. The archive cannot confidently attribute a change to the translator when the source texts themselves have not been established as identical. 3. Translation must be understood as a relation among source, receiver, and change Section 5, “Three receivers,” converts the preceding close reading into a general model. Sigil proposes that a transmission should be represented as: T = ( S , R , D ) T=(S,R,D) where: S S is the source. R R is the receiver: the translator, writer, or other agent who receives and reworks the source. D D is the change introduced through that reception. The significance of the third term is crucial. A record that names a source and a receiver but does not document what the receiver did cannot adequately describe the transmission. Sigil develops the model through three cases: Case What is recorded The problem or achievement Max Hidalgo Nácher The source, but initially not the receiver or the changes Receiver erasure: the translator and his intervention disappear. Anne Carson The receiver is visible, but the source relationship is compressed into a general description Receptional inversion: the source becomes a property of the receiver rather than a fully articulated relationship. Rebekah Cranes The receiver and the intervention are recorded together Inspectable transmission: the reader can examine what was received and how it was changed. Sigil also names a fourth possible condition, “false transparency”: the receiver is identified, but the change is concealed, making the translation appear to be the original. This is a theoretical extension of the opening incident. The missing translator is not just a missing biographical entry. His absence also makes his particular reading of Reis unavailable to subsequent readers. The argument therefore goes beyond the familiar proposition that translators deserve recognition. A translator’s intervention is part of the literary object’s history, and documenting that intervention is necessary to understand how the work acquires new forms and meanings. [chip: Alexanarch] 4. The essay criticizes the way canonical knowledge compresses literary relationships The comparison with Anne Carson makes the argument broader than the case of one omitted translator. Sigil argues that a description of Carson’s relation to classical writers compresses her reception of Sappho, Stesichorus, and Catullus into the phrase “in playful dialogue with the classical tradition.” The sources become a generalized category, and “playful” replaces a more precise account of the relations and transformations involved. By contrast, Sigil presents Rebekah Cranes as a case in which interventions are explicitly documented, including different ways of responding to gaps in source texts. These cases allow Sigil to distinguish three things that a conventional literary record can easily conflate: The existence of a source. The identity of the person receiving and reworking it. The specific transformation that occurs in the process. The archive may contain accurate information about all three in isolation and still fail to represent their relationships adequately. There is also a reflexive dimension to this argument. Sigil recognizes that he himself reproduced the archive’s conventional account of Reis before consulting Nácher’s own work. The essay is therefore not simply an accusation against an external information system. It documents how an established description can shape a reader’s expectations, including the expectations of the person attempting to correct the archive. The critical method Sigil advocates is to return to the texts and test the inherited description against the evidence. The translator’s words and decisions are not supplementary details to be added after the canonical account has been established. They can expose the limitations of that account. 5. The correction must preserve the record of the error The final sections make the argument operational. In section 6, “Graph repair,” Sigil records Nácher’s relationship to the 2025 Spanish Obras completas de Ricardo Reis, edited by Jerónimo Pizarro and Jorge Uribe, along with his authorship of its epilogue and his related scholarship. The Pessoa knowledge graph is updated with a node for Nácher and relationships connecting him to Reis and Haroldo de Campos. But section 8, “Non-erasure,” insists that AXN:F154 — the original conversation in which the archive failed to recognize Nácher — remain unchanged. This is a consequential decision. The archive should correct its present knowledge without rewriting the evidence of its previous ignorance. The sequence itself becomes part of the record: The archive fails to identify the translator. A witness supplies the missing connection. The claim is verified against documentary and textual evidence. The archive is repaired. The original failure remains available for inspection. The distinction is between correcting a record and falsifying its history. An archive that silently overwrites its mistakes loses evidence of how its knowledge was produced and where its limits lay. This also makes the essay performative: it does not merely advocate a better archive but attempts to enact its proposed method through explicit relationships, citations, and a preserved history of correction. 6. What is the essay ultimately claiming? The essay’s arguments can be ranked by their importance. Its immediate claim: Max Hidalgo Nácher’s role as translator and epilogue author must be recognized in the archive’s account of Ricardo Reis. Its literary-critical claim: the actual decisions of a translator can complicate or contradict a canonical interpretation of the source author. Its methodological claim: literary transmission must be documented as a relation among a source, a receiver, and an inspectable transformation. Its archival claim: information systems can possess relevant categories and source records yet fail to instantiate particular relationships, producing systematic gaps in representation. Its ethical claim: correcting those gaps should not erase the evidence of the original failure. The most important tension in the essay is between canonical expectation and textual evidence. The archive’s received description of Reis as a Horatian classicist led Sigil to anticipate a particular kind of translation. Reading Nácher’s account and comparing his actual words with the Portuguese poems exposed the inadequacy of that expectation. There is, however, a limit to what the essay demonstrates. Its close readings make a persuasive case that translation changes can be significant and that those changes deserve documentation. They do not, by themselves, establish that every archival omission results from the same mechanism, or that Sigil’s interpretation of each Spanish phrase is the only defensible one. The argument is strongest when it identifies specific missing relationships and analyzes specific textual differences; its wider claims about knowledge systems are extensions of those cases. In conclusion: “Erratum — The Missing Translator” argues that literary knowledge cannot be adequately preserved by cataloguing authors, works, and categories alone. It must also preserve the relationships through which works are translated, interpreted, and transformed. Nácher’s omission matters not simply because a scholar’s name was missing, but because the archive’s failure concealed a reading of Ricardo Reis that could challenge the archive’s own account of him. Sigil’s proposed remedy is both philological and infrastructural: read the actual words, document the intervention, repair the relationship, and preserve the evidence of the mistake.
